Does clone-censor-weighting carry modelling bias?

Modelling-bias QBA of the CCW analysis in the Maringe lung cancer example

Author

Artis Luguzis

Published

October 12, 2026

ImportantKey answer

The CCW analysis of the Maringe example carries a small but detectable modelling bias, its 95% CIs under-cover, and its type I error is inflated by about half. The QBA adjustments restore nominal coverage and type I error. The true CCW effect was set to the observed estimate and the study was replayed 100,000 times on the original 200 patients; a second set of 100,000 replays checked the case of no surgery effect.

CCW as published CCW + QBA adjustment

95% CI coverage (target 95%) 93.6% 94.8%
Type I error (target 5%) 7.483% 5.007%

Monte Carlo SE: about 0.2–0.3 percentage points for coverage and type I error, 0.006 for the bias. Bold cells differ from the target by more than their Monte Carlo error. Adjusted performance is cross-fitted (corrections estimated on one half of the replays, checked on the other).

  • Bias: the average estimate is HR 0.6121 instead of 0.6215, slightly too favourable to surgery (5% of one SE).
  • Coverage: the CIs cover the truth 93.6% of the time. The robust SE is 3.6% too small, and the misses are lopsided: 4.6% of CIs lie entirely below the true HR, 1.8% above.
  • Type I error: with no surgery effect, 7.483% of studies are significant, 6.267% of them in favour of surgery. Even with unlimited data the null CCW HR would be 0.9645.
  • Conclusion unchanged: the observed result was not significant (p = 0.072) and is less so after adjustment (p = 0.101).

What changed since the 5 October report: one dataset only (Maringe, as agreed for the paper); 100,000 instead of 5,000 replays per scenario; the censoring mechanism is addressed explicitly (Section 2.3); performance of the adjusted analysis is now evaluated, not only the adjusted estimate. The two-dataset report is kept in archive/2026-10-05_two_datasets/. Results agree with that run within Monte Carlo error.

1. What was done

The draft paper’s steps, applied to the published CCW analysis of Maringe et al. (2020):

Paper step What it means here
1. Fit the reference model Run the CCW analysis on the original data (Section 1.1).
2. Keep baseline data All covariates and each patient’s actual surgery date are kept unchanged.
3. Predict outcomes New death times from a Weibull model fitted to the data, in which surgery changes the hazard from the day it takes place. Surgery happens only if the patient is alive on that date. Censoring is predicted as well (Section 2.3). The surgery effect is calibrated so that the true CCW effect equals the observed estimate.
4. Repeat 100,000 replays per scenario; two scenarios: observed effect and no effect (200,000 CCW analyses; 2 failed).
5. Re-analyse The same CCW function as on the real data.
6. Quantify Bias, CI coverage, type I error and power, each with Monte Carlo SE.
7. Adjust Bias-corrected estimate, widened CI, calibrated critical value and p-value; their performance checked by cross-fitting.

1.1 Data and analysis

The dataset is the simulated example distributed with Maringe et al. (2020; ccwr::lungcancer): 200 elderly patients with stage I–II lung cancer, followed from diagnosis for one year. 106 had surgery (42 on day 1) and 48 died. It is not the registry cohort of their Table S2, but the table below uses the same layout.

Covariate balance at 6 months (as Figure S2 of Maringe et al.). Among clones still at risk at the end of the grace period, the arms differ strongly before weighting; the censoring weights reduce, but do not remove, these differences.

Before weighting, 10 of 11 covariate terms differ by more than 10% (largest 94.2%); after weighting, 4 still do (performance status 0 23.2%, age -17.5%, performance status 1 -12.5%, sex 11.9%). In the registry data of Maringe et al. all weighted differences were within 10%; in this 200-patient example the weight models leave residual imbalance. This is consistent with the no-effect scenario, where the CCW estimate stays below HR = 1 even with unlimited data (Section 2.2).

Computing time was 1884.9 minutes; with 1 parallel worker (crew 1.3.3, 4 cores available, R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24 ucrt)) the simulation stages took 18755.8 minutes of elapsed time. The 200 batches of simulated studies and the large datasets behind the true values run in parallel. The calibration search has 4 steps that follow each other, but the 12 large datasets within a step run in parallel, and its evaluations at θ* and 0 are reused for the true values (54.2 minutes of computing time). One CCW analysis of the 200 patients takes about 267 ms; the large datasets that define the true value take 13% of the computing time. Results do not depend on the number of workers: every replicate draws from its own seed.

2. How the simulation works

2.1 Simulate patients, not the CCW

CCW is an analysis procedure (cloning, artificial censoring, censoring weights, weighted outcome model), not a model of how outcomes arise, so nothing can be drawn from it directly:

  • The fitted CCW outcome model describes survival under two strategies: every patient appears in both arms, with one hazard ratio from day 0. A real patient has one history, and before surgery both strategies are identical for that patient.
  • The cloned dataset is not data: clones, artificial censoring and weights are produced by the analysis. Redrawing outcomes on the clones with weights held fixed would test only a weighted Cox fit, not CCW.

So the outcome-generating model is a patient-level model fitted to the original data: Weibull survival with surgery as a time-varying exposure, h(t) = h₀(t)·exp(γ′X + θ·1{t ≥ surgery date}). Covariates and surgery dates are kept (paper Step 2) and new death times are drawn. Each simulated dataset looks like the original data, and the whole CCW procedure is re-run on it.

2.2 Why the truth is not θ, and calibration

θ is the effect of surgery once received, at fixed covariates. The CCW hazard ratio compares strategies and differs from θ because of grace-period dilution (in the surgery arm patients are untreated until their surgery date), non-proportional strategy hazards, and non-collapsibility (the CCW model contains the strategy only). None of these has a closed form, so the truth ψ(θ) is computed numerically: the base data are copied to 50,000 patients, outcomes are simulated and the same CCW function is run; this is repeated 96 times and averaged.

θ is then searched until ψ(θ) equals the observed CCW estimate (paper Step 3):

Calibration path (secant search, 12 large datasets per step).
Step θ (log HR) Weibull HR exp(θ) ψ(θ), CCW log HR CCW HR
1 -0.415 0.6605 -0.307 0.7359
2 0.000 1.0000 -0.039 0.9614
3 -0.679 0.5070 -0.462 0.6300
4 -0.705 0.4941 -0.477 0.6206

Result: θ* = -0.705 (Weibull HR 0.4941), against the fitted coefficient θ = -0.415 (HR 0.6605). With 96 large datasets the truth is ψ(θ*) = -0.476 (HR 0.6215, MCSE 0.002), equal to the observed -0.477 within Monte Carlo error. The draft’s sentence “θ = −0.70, which results in HRCCW = 0.48” should read: θ* = −0.70 (Weibull HR 0.4941), which results in HRCCW = 0.6215.

No-effect scenario (θ = 0). Every patient’s outcome is then identical under both strategies, so every estimand is exactly null and the truth needs no estimation. The large-sample value ψ(0) = -0.036 is computed only as a diagnostic: it shows that CCW is off-centre even with unlimited data.

2.3 Censoring (paper Section 2.3)

The paper says that for time-to-event data the censoring distribution is also predicted, by switching the event/censoring indicator and modelling censoring dependent on covariates, and that the final times are the minimum of event and censoring times. This includes censoring after treatment start.

How the code does it. fit_dgm() fits a second Weibull model with the indicator switched: loss to follow-up is the event, deaths and the end of follow-up are censored. It uses the same covariates and surgery as a time-varying term, so censoring after treatment start has its own hazard. simulate_outcomes() draws a censoring time for each patient by the same inversion as the event time, from its own random numbers, and sets follow-up to min(event, censoring, end of study). This is controlled by censoring: model in config/config.yml and covered by unit tests.

Why it changes nothing for Maringe. In the original data all 152 survivors are followed to day 365.24: nobody is lost to follow-up. With the indicator switched there are no censoring events, so a censoring model cannot be fitted, and the predicted censoring distribution is the observed one: administrative censoring at one year for every patient. Maringe therefore runs with censoring: none, and the simulated data have exactly the original censoring pattern. Artificial censoring of clones is not part of this step: it is produced by the CCW analysis itself in every replay.

For the paper. Section 4 should state that the example has administrative censoring only. Two places in the draft disagree with Section 2.3 and could be aligned: the step figure (“keep … censoring times fixed”) and Table 1, row “Censoring” (“generated from a separately fitted censoring model”). For Maringe the two descriptions give the same simulated data, because the censoring model reduces to fixed administrative censoring.

3. Results

Bias. The average estimate is HR 0.6121 against a truth of 0.6215: a bias of -0.015 on the log scale (MC 95% interval -0.019 to -0.011), away from the null, detectable but small (5.4% of one SE).

Coverage. The empirical SE is 0.282, the average robust SE 0.272 (3.6% too small). Coverage is 93.6% (MCSE 0.1%), 92.5% with no effect. The SE shortfall and the bias alone would give about 94%; the rest comes from the lopsided misses: estimates and SEs are positively correlated, so low estimates get CIs that are too narrow. 4.6% of CIs lie entirely below the true HR and 1.8% above (6.3% and 1.2% with no effect; 2.5% each expected). This is the same asymmetry as the type I error.

Type I error. With no surgery effect, 7.483% (MCSE 0.083%) of studies reject H0: HR = 1 at 5%; 6.267% in favour of surgery and only 1.216% against it. The null estimates are centred at HR 0.9510, of which 0.9645 would remain with unlimited data, most likely because the censoring-weight models do not fully capture how surgery decisions depend on patient characteristics.

Power to detect the observed effect is 48.9%, consistent with the observed CI that includes 1.

Does the adjusted analysis work? Applying the adjustments estimated from half of the replays to the other half: coverage 94.8% (MCSE 0.1%), type I error 5.007% (MCSE 0.069%). Both are back at their targets. The price is lower power (42.7% instead of 48.9%), because part of the original power came from the inflated type I error.

4.1 Alternative CI: simulation bootstrap-t

The symmetric widening cannot correct the lopsided misses. An asymmetric CI uses the replays directly: the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of T=(ψ̂−ψ)/SÊT = (\hat\psi - \psi)/\widehat{SE} over the replays with true HR = observed are -2.25 and 1.84 (instead of ±1.96), and the CI is [ψ̂−q97.5SÊ,ψ̂−q2.5SÊ][\hat\psi - q_{97.5}\widehat{SE},\ \hat\psi - q_{2.5}\widehat{SE}]. This is a parametric bootstrap-t (Efron & Tibshirani 1993, ch. 12): the model fitted to the data generates the replays, and the observed estimate plays the role of the truth. TT already contains the bias, so the CI is built around the unadjusted estimate.

Observed result: HR 0.6206 (0.3811–1.1274), against Wald 0.3691–1.0433, QBA widening 0.3676–1.0798 and confidence belt 0.3715–1.1444 (Section 4.2).

How to read the checks. Both learned CIs are checked by cross-fitting (learned on half of the replays, checked on the other half). In the same scenario this is close to circular: the CI was tuned to exactly that distribution. The informative check is transfer: learn the CI at one true effect, check it at the other. It shows whether the CI still works when the true effect differs from the one used to build it, which is the situation of a real study.

Coverage of the 95% CIs, % (MCSE), and the share of CIs lying entirely below or above the truth (2.5% each expected). Confidence belt: coverage of the CCW large-sample limit, at no effect ψ(0) rather than 0 (Section 4.2).

  • Transfer (the real check): bootstrap-t 94.6% at no effect and 94.9% at the observed effect; QBA widening 93.9% and 94.7%; Wald 92.5% and 93.6%.
  • Why not exactly 95%: TT is not fully pivotal. Its quantiles shift with the true effect, so quantiles learned at one effect over-correct at the other (misses flip side in the transfer rows). Section 4.2 removes this assumption.
  • Validity rests on the same assumption as the rest of the QBA: the simulated world (Weibull outcome model, fixed covariates and surgery dates) is close enough to the real one.

4.2 Nominal CI: confidence belt

The bootstrap-t uses the quantiles of TT at one true effect. The confidence belt lets them depend on the true value (Neyman construction, test inversion):

  1. Grid of true effects. Besides θ* and 0, the study is replayed at 5 further values of θ, each with its own true value ψ(θ)\psi(\theta) (24 large datasets). The grid points are Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes in ψ over the range where CI endpoints fall (observed CI and the outer 0.5% of replicate Wald endpoints, widened by 10%), mapped to θ through a monotone spline of ψ(θ) through the calibration values, the true values and anchors at θ = ±2 and ±4 (3 large datasets each), and limited to the ψ values reached between the anchors. Each point gets 1,000 replays first (same seeds), then more until the Monte Carlo SE of both quantiles of TT is below 0.02 (at most 30,000): 21,000 to 30,000 replays per point.
  2. Quantile curves. At each grid point, the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of T=(ψ̂−ψ)/SÊT = (\hat\psi - \psi)/\widehat{SE}; a weighted polynomial in ψ\psi (degree 3) smooths them across the grid (figure below).
  3. Inversion. The CI is every ψ0\psi_0 with q2.5(ψ0)≤(ψ̂−ψ0)/SÊ≤q97.5(ψ0)q_{2.5}(\psi_0) \le (\hat\psi - \psi_0)/\widehat{SE} \le q_{97.5}(\psi_0), i.e. every true value that a 5% test calibrated at that value would not reject.

Why nominal: for any true value, the test calibrated at it rejects 5% of the time, so the set of non-rejected values contains the truth 95% of the time, whatever the true effect, without assuming TT is pivotal. What remains is Monte Carlo error in the quantiles, smoothing between grid points, and the adequacy of the simulated world.

Check. A CI covers ψ0\psi_0 exactly when the test at ψ0\psi_0 does not reject, so with the checked effect on the grid coverage would hold by construction. The check therefore drops that grid point and refits the curves (and cross-fits over replays), so the belt has to interpolate, as it would for an unknown true effect. The MCSEs come from a bootstrap over replays (200 resamples, replays resampled jointly across grid points) and include the Monte Carlo error of the grid quantiles, not only the binomial error of the checked CIs (0.07%):

  • Observed effect: coverage 94.8% (MCSE 0.1%); 2.6% of CIs entirely below the truth, 2.6% above.
  • No effect: coverage of ψ(0) = -0.036 (HR 0.9645), the CCW large-sample limit when surgery has no effect, 95.1% (MCSE 0.1%); 2.4% below, 2.5% above. The belt is indexed by the CCW limit at every grid point, so here it targets ψ(0) rather than the convention 0 used for the type I error (Section 2.2); whether a belt CI excludes HR = 1 is therefore not a test of no effect.
  • Grid range: 18% (observed) and 1% (no effect) of replay CIs have an endpoint beyond the grid, where the nearest quantile is used. The grid runs at most from θ = −4 to 4: for strong effects ψ(θ) levels off (deaths before surgery stay in the surgery arm), so no θ in this range gives a CCW HR below HR 0.2777. This affects the far endpoint only, not whether the CI contains the truth.

6. Caveats and next steps

  • Truths are simulated (MCSE 0.002); this is included in the bias interval.
  • Adjusted bias is zero by construction under two-fold cross-fitting; coverage and type I error of the adjusted analysis are genuine checks.
  • The null offset (ψ(0) ≠ 0) suggests the censoring-weight models are not flexible enough; a sensitivity analysis with splines for age and deprivation in the weight models would test this.
  • The Word draft of paper Section 4 (reports/paper/section4_draft.docx) uses the same results.

A2. Data-generating mechanism

Kept fixed from the original data (paper Step 2): covariates XiX_i and each patient’s surgery date sis_i (si=∞s_i = \infty if not operated). Censoring: Ci=365.24C_i = 365.24 for all patients (no loss to follow-up; Section 2.3).

Outcome model. Weibull proportional hazards with surgery as a time-varying exposure:

hi(t)=λρtρ−1exp⁡{γ⊤Xi+θI(t≥si)},ηi=log⁡λ+γ⊤Xi,h_i(t) = \lambda \rho\, t^{\rho - 1} \exp\{\gamma^\top X_i + \theta\, I(t \ge s_i)\}, \qquad \eta_i = \log\lambda + \gamma^\top X_i,

Hi(t)=eηi[min(t,si)ρ+eθmax{0,tρ−siρ}].H_i(t) = e^{\eta_i}\left[\min(t, s_i)^{\rho} + e^{\theta}\,\max\{0,\; t^{\rho} - s_i^{\rho}\}\right].

In simulation, log⁡λ\log\lambda, ρ\rho and γ\gamma are kept at their fitted values and θ\theta is set to the scenario value (θ*\theta^* or 0). Where a censoring model is fitted, it has the same form with the indicator switched (1−δi1 - \delta_i for loss to follow-up).

Simulation by inversion (common random numbers: UiU_i depends only on the replicate seed, not on θ\theta). With Ei=−log⁡UiE_i = -\log U_i:

Ti={(Eie−ηi)1/ρif Ei≤eηisiρ (death before surgery),{siρ+(Ei−eηisiρ)e−ηi−θ}1/ρotherwise.T_i = \begin{cases} \left(E_i\, e^{-\eta_i}\right)^{1/\rho} & \text{if } E_i \le e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho} \text{ (death before surgery)},\\[4pt] \left\{ s_i^{\rho} + \left(E_i - e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho}\right) e^{-\eta_i - \theta} \right\}^{1/\rho} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}

R code: Weibull fit, censoring model and simulation (R/dgm.R) 
#' Fit the reference DGM (outcome and censoring models) to the base data
#' @param data Base data from `prepare_base_data()`.
#' @param spec `cfg$dgm`; @param cens_spec `cfg$censoring` (model: none, fixed or weibull).
#' @return Outcome-model list (see `fit_weibull_tv()`) with element `cens`.
fit_dgm <- function(data, spec, cens_spec = list(model = "fixed")) {
  checkmate::assert_data_table(data)
  checkmate::assert_choice(cens_spec$model, c("none", "fixed", "weibull"))
  dgm <- fit_weibull_tv(data, spec$covariates, data$status)
  # Censoring model: loss to follow-up is the event; outcome events and the horizon censor it
  dgm$cens <- if (cens_spec$model == "weibull") {
    c(list(model = "weibull"), fit_weibull_tv(data, cens_spec$covariates, data$cens_event))
  } else {
    list(model = cens_spec$model)
  }
  dgm
}

#' Invert the piecewise Weibull cumulative hazard (switch to exp(theta) at time s)
#' @param eta Linear predictor incl. intercept; @param rho Shape; @param theta Log-HR on treatment.
#' @param s Planned treatment time; @param u Uniforms.
#' @return Simulated times; the same u gives times monotone in theta.
invert_weibull_tv <- function(eta, rho, theta, s, u) {
  E <- -log(u)
  h_pre <- exp(eta) * s^rho
  data.table::fifelse(
    E <= h_pre,
    (E / exp(eta))^(1 / rho),
    (s^rho + (E - h_pre) / exp(eta + theta))^(1 / rho)
  )
}

#' Simulate event (and censoring) times for fixed baseline data and treatment plans
#' @param data Base data (covariates and planned treatment time `s` are kept).
#' @param dgm Fitted DGM from `fit_dgm()`.
#' @param theta Treatment log-HR used for simulation.
#' @param u,u_cens Uniforms for event and censoring times, one per patient (CRN).
#' @return Copy of `data` with simulated `time`, `status`, `cens_time`, `trt_time`.
simulate_outcomes <- function(data, dgm, theta, u, u_cens = NULL) {
  checkmate::assert_numeric(u, len = nrow(data), lower = 0, upper = 1)
  X <- dgm_design(data, dgm$covariates)
  t_ev <- invert_weibull_tv(dgm$alpha + drop(X %*% dgm$gamma), dgm$rho, theta, data$s, u)
  out <- data.table::copy(data)
  cm <- if (is.null(dgm$cens)) "fixed" else dgm$cens$model
  if (cm == "weibull") {
    checkmate::assert_numeric(u_cens, len = nrow(data), lower = 0, upper = 1)
    cs <- dgm$cens
    Xc <- dgm_design(data, cs$covariates)
    # Censoring hazard also changes at treatment start; theta_c is kept as fitted
    eta_c <- cs$alpha + drop(Xc %*% cs$gamma)
    t_c <- invert_weibull_tv(eta_c, cs$rho, cs$theta_hat, data$s, u_cens)
    out[, cens_time := pmin(t_c, admin_time)]
  }
  out[, `:=`(time = pmin(t_ev, cens_time), status = as.integer(t_ev <= cens_time))]
  out[, trt_time := data.table::fifelse(s <= time, s, Inf)]
  out[]
}

A3. Censoring weights and outcome model

Grace period g=182.62g = 182.62 days; ZZ = age, sex, performance status, stage, deprivation, Charlson index, emergency presentation.

  • Arm 0, no surgery within gg. Censored at surgery: Cia=siC^a_i = s_i if si≤min⁡(g,Yi)s_i \le \min(g, Y_i). Cox model for time to surgery with Breslow baseline; weights updated at every distinct surgery date: Wi(t)=1Ŝc(t∣Zi)=exp⁡{Λ̂0c(min(t,g))eβ̂⊤Zi}.W_i(t) = \frac{1}{\hat S^c(t \mid Z_i)} = \exp\left\{\hat\Lambda^c_0\big(\min(t, g)\big)\, e^{\hat\beta^\top Z_i}\right\}.
  • Arm 1, surgery within gg. Censored at gg if alive and not operated. Logistic model among patients alive at gg, π(Z)=P(s≤g∣Z,Y>g)\pi(Z) = P(s \le g \mid Z, Y > g): Wi(t)=1 for t<g,Wi(t)=1/π̂(Zi) for t≥g.W_i(t) = 1 \text{ for } t < g, \qquad W_i(t) = 1/\hat\pi(Z_i) \text{ for } t \ge g.
  • Outcome model. Weighted Cox model on the stacked clones, λ(t∣A)=λ0(t)eψA\lambda(t \mid A) = \lambda_0(t)\, e^{\psi A}, Efron ties, robust SE clustered on patient, Wald 95% CI.
R code: cloning, weights and outcome model (R/pipeline.R) 
#' Clone into "surgery within grace" (arm 1) and "no surgery within grace" (arm 0)
#' @param data Patient-level data; @param grace Grace period (days).
#' @return Clone rows: arm, end, event, art_cens.
build_clones <- function(data, grace) {
  ctrl <- data.table::copy(data)[, arm := 0L]
  ctrl[, art_cens := as.integer(trt_time <= grace)]
  ctrl[, `:=`(
    end = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, trt_time, time),
    event = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, 0L, status)
  )]
  surg <- data.table::copy(data)[, arm := 1L]
  # Deaths before grace without surgery stay in the surgery arm (Maringe et al. 2020)
  surg[, art_cens := as.integer(trt_time > grace & time > grace)]
  surg[, `:=`(
    end = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, grace, time),
    event = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, 0L, status)
  )]
  data.table::rbindlist(list(ctrl, surg))
}

#' Inverse probability of censoring weights for the control arm (Cox censoring model)
#' @param clones Control-arm clones; @param spec Pipeline spec.
#' @return Long data split at censoring times, with weight `w` = 1 / P(uncensored at start).
weight_control <- function(clones, spec) {
  f <- stats::reformulate(spec$cens_covariates, response = "survival::Surv(end, art_cens)")
  fit <- survival::coxph(f, data = clones, ties = "breslow")
  bh <- survival::basehaz(fit, centered = FALSE)
  clones[, lp := stats::predict(fit, type = "lp", reference = "zero")]
  # Split at the observed censoring (surgery) times: weights change only there
  ctimes <- sort(unique(clones[art_cens == 1L, end]))
  brk <- unique(c(0, ctimes[ctimes < spec$grace], spec$grace))
  long <- split_clones(clones, brk)
  H0 <- stats::stepfun(bh$time, c(0, bh$hazard))
  # Right-continuous: those censored at a break have left the risk set
  long[, w := exp(H0(pmin(start, spec$grace)) * exp(lp))]
  long[]
}

#' Inverse probability of censoring weights for the surgery arm
#' @param clones Surgery-arm clones; @param data Patient data; @param spec Pipeline spec.
#' @return Long data split at grace, with weight `w`.
weight_surgery <- function(clones, data, spec) {
  long <- split_clones(clones, c(0, spec$grace))
  # Censoring happens only at grace end, for patients alive and not yet operated
  alive <- data[time > spec$grace]
  alive[, op := as.integer(trt_time <= spec$grace)]
  f <- stats::reformulate(spec$cens_covariates, response = "op")
  fit <- stats::glm(f, family = stats::binomial(), data = alive)
  alive[, p_op := stats::predict(fit, type = "response")]
  long[, w := 1]
  long[alive, on = "id", p_op := i.p_op]
  long[start >= spec$grace, w := 1 / p_op]
  long[]
}

#' Weighted Cox model for the strategy contrast
#' @param long Stacked long data (id, arm, start, stop, ev, w); @param spec Pipeline spec.
#' @param robust Robust (cluster) SE; FALSE only for large-sample truth runs.
#' @return One-row data.table in the pipeline contract format.
fit_outcome <- function(long, spec, robust) {
  fit <- if (robust) {
    survival::coxph(
      survival::Surv(start, stop, ev) ~ arm,
      data = long, weights = w, cluster = id, ties = "efron"
    )
  } else {
    survival::coxph(survival::Surv(start, stop, ev) ~ arm, data = long, weights = w, ties = "efron")
  }
  est <- unname(stats::coef(fit)["arm"])
  se <- unname(sqrt(stats::vcov(fit)["arm", "arm"]))
  z <- stats::qnorm(1 - (1 - spec$conf_level) / 2)
  data.table::data.table(
    estimate = est, se = se, ci_lo = est - z * se, ci_hi = est + z * se,
    p_value = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(est / se)), n_events = sum(long$ev),
    status = "ok", message = NA_character_
  )
}

A4. True value, calibration, performance and adjustment

  • Truth: ψ̃(θ)=1R∑r=1Rψ̂N(r)\tilde\psi(\theta) = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} \hat\psi^{(r)}_N, with N=50,000N = 50,000 and R=96R = 96.
  • Calibration: θ*\theta^* solves ψ̃(θ)=ψ̂obs\tilde\psi(\theta) = \hat\psi_{\text{obs}} (secant search from θ̂\hat\theta and 0, 12 large datasets per step run in parallel, tolerance 0.005; the same seeds at every θ, so the evaluations at θ* and 0 are the first 12 of the 96 large datasets of the true values).
  • Performance over B=100,000B = 100,000 replicates: bias =ψ̂‾−ψ= \bar{\hat\psi} - \psi; coverage =B−1∑bI(|ψ̂b−ψ|≤1.96SÊb)= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b - \psi| \le 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b); rejection rate =B−1∑bI(|ψ̂b|>1.96SÊb)= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b| > 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b). The MCSE of the bias includes the truth’s MC error.
  • Adjustment: ψ̂adj=ψ̂−biaŝ\hat\psi^{adj} = \hat\psi - \widehat{\text{bias}}; CI ψ̂adj±1.96kSÊ\hat\psi^{adj} \pm 1.96\, k\, \widehat{SE} with k=max⁡(1,SEemp/SEmod)k = \max(1, SE_{emp}/SE_{mod}); critical value z*z^* = 95th percentile of |z||z| under θ=0\theta = 0. Two-fold cross-fitting over replicate index for the adjusted performance.
  • Confidence belt: indexed by the CCW large-sample limit ψ(θ) at every grid point, including ψ(0) at no effect; grid of Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes in ψ (endpoints included, 5 nodes, nodes within 0.05 of a main-scenario truth dropped); replays per node added in batches until the order-statistic MCSE of both quantiles is below 0.02; grid quantiles qa(ψj)q_a(\psi_j) of (ψ̂b−ψj)/SÊb(\hat\psi_b - \psi_j)/\widehat{SE}_b (type 8), smoothed by a weighted polynomial in ψ\psi (weights = replays; constant beyond the grid); CI ={ψ0:q2.5(ψ0)≤(ψ̂−ψ0)/SÊ≤q97.5(ψ0)}= \{\psi_0: q_{2.5}(\psi_0) \le (\hat\psi - \psi_0)/\widehat{SE} \le q_{97.5}(\psi_0)\} by bisection. Check: leave the checked grid point out, two-fold cross-fitting over replicate index.
  • Bootstrap-t CI: [ψ̂−q97.5SÊ,ψ̂−q2.5SÊ][\hat\psi - q_{97.5}\widehat{SE},\ \hat\psi - q_{2.5}\widehat{SE}], qaq_a = quantile of (ψ̂b−ψ)/SÊb(\hat\psi_b - \psi)/\widehat{SE}_b over the replicates at θ*\theta^* (type 8). Transfer check: quantiles learned at θ*\theta^* applied at θ=0\theta = 0 and vice versa.
R code: truth and calibration (R/truth.R) 
#' CCW estimate on one large dataset (one truth seed at one theta)
#' @param dgm Fitted DGM; @param data Base data; @param theta Treatment log-HR in the DGM.
#' @param seed_id Index into `seeds`; @param seeds Truth seeds from `make_crn_seeds()`.
#' @param pipeline Pipeline spec; @param cfg Full config (uses `truth$n_target`).
#' @param known Earlier evaluations (theta, seed_id, estimate, n_truth) to reuse, or NULL.
#' @return One-row data.table: theta, seed_id, estimate, n_truth.
truth_point <- function(dgm, data, theta, seed_id, seeds, pipeline, cfg, known = NULL) {
  checkmate::assert_number(theta)
  checkmate::assert_int(seed_id, lower = 1, upper = length(seeds))
  if (!is.null(known) && nrow(known)) {
    # Local copies: inside data.table's [ ] the bare names would refer to the columns
    th <- theta
    sid <- seed_id
    hit <- known[abs(theta - th) < 1e-10 & seed_id == sid]
    if (nrow(hit)) return(hit[1, .(theta, seed_id, estimate, n_truth)])
  }
  big <- stack_copies(data, ceiling(cfg$truth$n_target / nrow(data)))
  rng <- draw_replicate_rng(seeds[seed_id], nrow(big))
  sim <- simulate_outcomes(big, dgm, theta, rng$u_event, rng$u_cens)
  data.table::data.table(
    theta = theta, seed_id = seed_id,
    estimate = run_pipeline(sim, pipeline, robust = FALSE)$estimate, n_truth = nrow(big)
  )
}

#' Starting values of the calibration search (paper Step 3)
#' @param dgm Fitted DGM; @param min_gap Smallest |theta_hat| for which 0 is the second start.
#' @return Two theta values.
calib_start <- function(dgm, min_gap = 0.25) {
  th <- dgm$theta_hat
  # psi(0) is needed anyway as the null-scenario truth, so 0 is a free second start; it is
  # only uninformative for the secant when theta_hat is itself close to 0
  if (abs(th) >= min_gap) c(th, 0) else c(th, th - 0.5)
}

#' Next calibration point from all evaluations so far
#' @param rows From `truth_point()`; @param target Observed CCW estimate.
#' @param cc `cfg$calibration` (tol, bound).
#' @return Scalar theta: the best point so far once within tol, else a secant step.
calib_next <- function(rows, target, cc) {
  checkmate::assert_number(target, finite = TRUE)
  checkmate::assert_number(cc$tol, lower = 0)
  checkmate::assert_number(cc$bound, lower = 0)
  ps <- summarise_truth(rows)
  ps[, gap := truth - target]
  best <- ps[which.min(abs(gap))]
  if (abs(best$gap) < cc$tol || nrow(ps) < 2) return(best$theta)
  # Interpolate between the closest points bracketing the target, else secant through the
  # two closest points; psi is smooth and monotone in theta under CRN
  lo <- ps[gap < 0][which.max(gap)]
  hi <- ps[gap > 0][which.min(gap)]
  pair <- if (nrow(lo) && nrow(hi)) rbind(lo, hi) else ps[order(abs(gap))][1:2]
  slope <- diff(pair$truth) / diff(pair$theta)
  th <- pair$theta[1] + (target - pair$truth[1]) / slope
  if (!is.finite(th)) return(best$theta)
  max(-cc$bound, min(cc$bound, th))
}

#' Finish the calibration: serial secant steps if the parallel stages did not converge
#' @param rows Evaluations from the parallel stages; @param dgm,data,pipeline,cfg As above.
#' @param obs_result Observed pipeline result; @param seeds Truth seeds.
#' @param n_stages Parallel refinement stages already run (count towards `max_iter`).
#' @return List: theta_star, psi_star, at_bound, path (search history), evals (all rows).
finish_calibration <- function(rows, dgm, data, obs_result, pipeline, cfg, seeds, n_stages = 2L) {
  cc <- cfg$calibration
  target <- obs_result$estimate
  ids <- seq_len(cc$n_rep)
  for (i in seq_len(max(0L, cc$max_iter - n_stages))) {
    th <- calib_next(rows, target, cc)
    if (any(abs(rows$theta - th) < 1e-10)) break
    rows <- rbind(rows, data.table::rbindlist(lapply(ids, function(j) {
      truth_point(dgm, data, th, j, seeds, pipeline, cfg)
    })))
  }
  ps <- summarise_truth(rows, ids)
  best <- ps[which.min(abs(truth - target))]
  # Order of first evaluation = search order
  first <- unique(rows[, .(theta)])
  path <- ps[match(first$theta, ps$theta), .(step = seq_len(.N), theta, psi = truth)]
  list(
    theta_star = best$theta,
    psi_star = best$truth,
    at_bound = abs(best$theta) >= cc$bound,
    path = path,
    evals = rows
  )
}
